title: Class 6 Maths Mean Median Mode Explained (With a Worked Case Study) + Free Quiz
meta_title: Class 6 Maths Mean Median Mode Explained + Free Quiz
meta_desc: Learn class 6 maths mean median mode with clear rules, a solved marks case study, range explained, and a free 8-question quiz to test your child.
excerpt: Mean, median and mode confuse a lot of Class 6 students because all three get called 'the average'. Here is the plain-English version, one solved marks case study, and a quick quiz to check understanding.
author: Sachin Sharma
content:
Hand a Class 6 student the marks 8, 9, 7, 9, 10, 6, 9 and ask for ‘the average’, and most will add and divide without a second thought. Ask instead which mark was most common, or which one sits bang in the middle, and you get puzzled looks. That gap is exactly what the class 6 maths mean median mode chapter is about — three different ways to describe one set of numbers with a single value, each answering a slightly different question. Get the difference clear now and statistics stays easy for years.

These three are called measures of central tendency, which is a fancy name for a plain idea: a single number that stands in for a whole list. Let me take them one at a time, then walk through a real marks case study the way it appears in an exam.

Mean: the everyday average

The mean is the one children already half-know. You add up all the values and divide by how many there are.

For the marks 8, 9, 7, 9, 10, 6, 9: the sum is 58, and there are 7 marks, so the mean is 58 ÷ 7 = 8.28 (roughly). Notice the mean need not be a whole number, and it need not match any actual mark on the list. That surprises a lot of students the first time.

The mean is the right choice when the values are fairly close together — test scores, daily temperatures, heights in a class. Its one weakness: a single odd value drags it. One student scoring 2 out of 10 pulls the class mean down more than it deserves. Keep that caveat in your back pocket; it comes up later.

Median: the middle value

The median is simply the middle number once you line the values up in order. The ordering step is the part students skip and then get wrong.

Take 8, 9, 7, 9, 10, 6, 9. Sorted, that is 6, 7, 8, 9, 9, 9, 10. Seven numbers, so the fourth one is the middle: the median is 9.

The two-middle case

What if there is an even count, with no single middle? Then you take the two central values and find their mean. For 6, 7, 8, 9, 9, 9, 10, 11 (eight numbers), the two middle values are the 4th and 5th — 9 and 9 — so the median is (9 + 9) ÷ 2 = 9. If the two middles had been 8 and 10, the median would be 9 as well: (8 + 10) ÷ 2. This even-count rule is the single most tested detail in the chapter, so drill it.

Mode: the most frequent value

The mode is the value that appears most often. In 6, 7, 8, 9, 9, 9, 10, the number 9 shows up three times, more than any other, so the mode is 9. A list can have no mode (every value appears once), or more than one mode if two values tie. The mode is the only one of the three that works for things you cannot add — the most common shoe size sold, the favourite colour in a class.

Range: the spread, not the centre

Range is not a measure of centre, but it lives in the same chapter, so know it. The range is the largest value minus the smallest. For our marks, 10 − 6 = 4. It tells you how spread out the marks are, nothing about where the middle sits.

When to use which

Here is the comparison I put on the board and never rub off:

MeasureWhat it tells youBest used whenFor 6, 7, 8, 9, 9, 9, 10
MeanThe balancing averageValues are close, no extreme outlier8.28
MedianThe middle valueOne or two values are unusually high or low9
ModeThe most common valueYou want the most typical or popular choice9
RangeThe spreadYou care how far apart the values are4

Worked case study: Riya’s weekly maths quiz

This is the kind of passage the exam gives you, so read it the way you would read a real question.

Passage. Riya scored the following marks (out of 10) in her seven daily maths quizzes one week: Monday 7, Tuesday 8, Wednesday 6, Thursday 9, Friday 8, Saturday 10, Sunday 8. Her teacher wants a single number to describe her week.

  • Find the mean. Sum = 7 + 8 + 6 + 9 + 8 + 10 + 8 = 56. There are 7 marks, so mean = 56 ÷ 7 = 8. Riya averages 8 out of 10.
  • Find the median. Order the marks: 6, 7, 8, 8, 8, 9, 10. Seven values, so the middle (fourth) is 8. Median = 8.
  • Find the mode. The value 8 appears three times, more than any other. Mode = 8.
  • Find the range. Largest − smallest = 10 − 6 = 4.

Here mean, median and mode all land on 8 — which happens when marks are evenly balanced, and it is a good sign her performance is steady. Now change one number: suppose Saturday had been 2 instead of 10. The mean drops to 50 ÷ 7 = 7.14, but the median stays at 8. That is the counter-intuitive lesson worth remembering — when one value goes rogue, the median holds steady while the mean lurches. That is precisely why cricket commentators quote a median-like ‘typical’ score rather than a mean skewed by one big innings.

Try the quiz, then the case-study book

The eight questions below cover mean, median (including the two-middle case), mode and range at Class 6 level. Attempt each, then read the explanation for any you miss. quiz.intro: Eight quick questions on mean, median, mode and range. Pick an answer for each, then press Check my score.

questions.q: What is the mean of 4, 8 and 6?
questions.explanation: Add them: 4 + 8 + 6 = 18. There are 3 values, so the mean is 18 ÷ 3 = 6.
Order first: 1, 3, 5, 7, 9. Five values, so the middle (third) one is 5.
The mode is the value that appears most often. 3 appears twice, more than any other.

questions.q: What is the range of 12, 4, 9 and 7?

questions.explanation: An even count has two middle values, 4 and 6. Their mean is (4 + 6) ÷ 2 = 5.

options: The sum of the values divided by how many there are
The largest value minus the smallest
questions.explanation: Mean = sum of all values ÷ number of values. The other options describe mode, median and range.
10 appears three times, more often than any other value, so the mode is 10.

questions.q: Aarav scored 8, 9, 7, 9, 9 in five spelling tests. What is the mode of his marks?
questions.explanation: The mark 9 appears three times, more than any other, so the mode is 9.

faq.q: What is the difference between mean, median and mode?
faq.a: The mean is the sum of the values divided by how many there are. The median is the middle value once the numbers are put in order. The mode is the value that appears most often. All three describe a data set with one number, but they answer different questions.

faq.q: How do you find the median when there is an even number of values?
faq.a: Order the values, then take the two middle ones and find their mean. For 4, 6, 8, 10 the two middle values are 6 and 8, so the median is (6 + 8) ÷ 2 = 7.

faq.q: Can a data set have more than one mode?
faq.a: Yes. If two values tie for the most appearances, the set has two modes. If every value appears the same number of times, there is no mode at all.

faq.q: Why does the median sometimes describe data better than the mean?
faq.a: When one value is unusually high or low, it drags the mean up or down, but the median barely moves. So for lists with an odd extreme value — like one very high test score — the median gives a fairer sense of the typical value.
